Introduction

  • A chronic, transmural inflammatory disease of the gastrointestinal tract of unknown cause.
  • Crohn's disease can involve any part of the alimentary tract from the mouth to the anus but most commonly affects the small intestine, colon, rectum & anus.
Notes

Indeterminate Colitis

Definition
Indeterminate colitis = isolated colonic disease confined to the colon, where features do not clearly fit either Crohn's disease (CD) or ulcerative colitis (UC).
  • Proven colon-cancer risk factor → ulcerative colitis. 429 ×3
Notes

Crohn's Disease Definition

Crohn's disease = chronic transmural inflammation that may involve any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus; most commonly affects the small bowel and/or colon.
  • The goal of surgical treatment of Crohn’s disease is to provide long-lasting symptomatic relief while avoiding excessive morbidity.
  • Crohn’s disease cannot be cured by surgical therapy,
    • Surgery, like medical treatment, should be considered palliative.
  • The main aims of surgical treatment is the treatment of complications and palliation of symptoms while avoiding excessive loss of intestine.
Notes

Role of Surgery

Key Concept
Surgery in Crohn's is palliative, NOT curative — it aims for long-lasting symptomatic relief and treatment of complications. Crohn's cannot be cured surgically.
Surgery should be as conservative as possible to avoid repeated bowel loss and short bowel syndrome.
Main principle: remove/treat only the segment causing the clinical problem — do not resect every visibly inflamed segment if it is asymptomatic.
Selected isolated disease may sometimes be treated surgically, but the general principle remains: surgery is not curative.
Crohn's surgery is palliative, not curative — be conservative; remove only the segment causing the problem (avoid short bowel syndrome).
  • 40 cm small-bowel resection 2 years ago, now diarrhoea, weight loss, malnutrition → keyed short bowel syndrome. 442
Notes

Complications / Surgical Indications Main Complications

Obstruction / stricture
Perforation
Fistula
GI bleeding
Malignancy
Failure to thrive / severe nutritional consequences (esp. children)
Acute / Emergency Surgical Indications
Established obstruction
Free perforation
Significant GI bleeding
Important fistulous disease (e.g., enterovesical/colovesical fistula)
Malignancy
Severe nutritional consequences / failure of medical management
  • Optimal surgical therapy may require leaving behind segments of the intestinal tract affected by mild but asymptomatic disease with resection of only the areas of severe and symptomatic Crohn’s disease.
Notes

Fistulas

Key Rule
Not every Crohn's fistula requires surgery — asymptomatic fistulas may be observed.

Pathogenesis: chronic transmural inflammation → bowel adheres to an adjacent structure → inflammatory mass/abscess → penetration into adjacent organ → fistula.

Small bowel ↔ colon/other bowel loops
Bowel → adjacent abdominal organs
Bowel → skin (enterocutaneous fistula)
Bowel → urinary bladder (enterovesical fistula)
Surgical Principle
Treat the diseased Crohn's segment while preserving an adjacent organ that is only secondarily involved, whenever possible.
Notes

Example: Ileosigmoid Fistula

ScenarioManagement
Sigmoid is healthy / not primarily diseasedResect diseased ileum + repair/close sigmoid defect; do not unnecessarily resect sigmoid
Both segments have true Crohn's diseaseBoth diseased segments may require resection
Notes

Bladder Involvement

Crohn's primarily affects the GI tract, not bladder mucosa itself. With an enterovesical fistula → resect the diseased bowel; repair the bladder defect as required rather than unnecessarily removing healthy bladder tissue.
  • Weeks of pain, fever and diarrhoea, then an enterocutaneous fistula in the RLQ → Crohn's disease. 439 ×4

Bad prognostic features

  • Diagnosis below the age of 40 years,
  • Smoker,
  • Perianal disease,
  • Stricturing disease,
  • Sever loss of weight (BMI 13)
Notes

Poor Prognostic Features in Crohn's

Diagnosis at <40 years
Smoking
Perianal disease
Stricturing disease
Severe weight loss
Warning Signs

Complications

  • Obstruction
  • Perforation.
  • Fistulas occur between the sites of perforation and adjacent organs, such as loops of small and large intestine, the urinary bladder, the vagina, the stomach, and sometimes the skin,
  • Localized abscesses.
  • Toxic megacolon in patients with Crohn's colitis.
  • Cancer
  • Post-hemicolectomy local peritonitis in Crohn's → anastomotic leak. 439

Indications for surgery

  • Most common indication for surgery in Crohn's → intestinal obstruction. 432 ×3
  • Indication for immediate laparotomy in Crohn's → free perforation. 438 ×11
  • Crohn's with a complex fistula and 4-cm perianal abscess → incision and drainage + seton (never fistulotomy for complex Crohn's fistulas). 439

Workup

  • Clinical: Hx & Ex
  • Blood work:
    • CBC, U&E, LFT, Coagulation profile,
    • Inflammatory markers CRP, ESR ( may be Normal because

1. Stricture disease

2. overused

  • ANCA & ASCA
  • Nutritional Albumin, prealbumin , Wt is the most important feature for nutritional assessment
  • Stool: Culture & microscopy to R/O infectious colitis
  • C diff toxin to R/O pseudomembranous colitis
Notes

Workup of Crohn's / IBD Patient Basic Assessment

History + physical examination are mandatory in every patient.
Basic investigations: CBC, U&E/renal profile, liver/hepatic profile, coagulation profile, CRP ± ESR.
Add disease-specific tests when appropriate (e.g., tumor markers if malignancy suspected).
Nutritional assessment is important, particularly before surgery.
Notes

Stool Studies

Fecal Calprotectin — Key Rule of Thumb
LevelInterpretation
> 50 µg/gRaises suspicion for intestinal inflammation / IBD
< 50 µg/gIBD becomes much less likely
likely.Not specific for IBD — other inflammatory/infectious colitides can elevate it. High calprotectin without an obvious infectious cause makes IBD more
Stool culture + microscopy → exclude infectious causes of colitis (viral or bacterial).
Always consider/exclude C. difficile.
  • IBD patient (mild colitis a year ago) now with haematochezia → flare of IBD (Crohn's). 441
  • UGI scope & Colonoscopy with biopsy
  • MR enterography
  • The whole GI tract must be invistegated.
  • Gold standard to diagnose IBD → colonoscopy with multiple biopsies. 442
Notes

Evaluating the Entire GI Tract

Because Crohn's may involve anywhere from mouth to anus, the whole GI tract must be assessed, especially before surgery.

Upper GI endoscopy
Lower GI endoscopy/colonoscopy
MR enterography (MRE)
CT enterography (CTE)

Purpose: map disease distribution and plan the most appropriate surgical treatment.

Preop preparation

  • The whole GI study
  • Consult gastroenterologist
  • Ureterci stent
  • 2 cm gross healthy margin
Notes

Preoperative Preparation in Crohn's

Usual surgical pre-op preparation, plus:
Gastroenterology consultation
Complete GI tract mapping
Nutritional optimization
Stoma site marking (if stoma may be required)
Consider Ureteric Stents
Crohn's inflammation, abscesses, collections and adhesions can make ureters difficult to identify intraoperatively. Preoperative stents help identify/protect the ureters in difficult pelvic/inflammatory surgery.

Resection Vs stricturoplasty

  • Index case surgery
    • Risk of short bowel syndrome Stricturoplasty
  • Anastomosis Vs stoma
    • Abscess or steroid prefer stoma
  • Fistulizing disease
    • The diseased segment to be resected
    • The non diseased segment just repair
  • Contraindication to stricturoplasty → a fistula (or abscess) at the stricture. 431
Notes

Resection Margin

Key Rule
Crohn's does not require wide oncological margins. Approximately 2 cm of grossly healthy bowel proximal/distal to the diseased segment is usually sufficient. Margin is based on grossly healthy appearance — avoid extensive bowel removal.
  • Two strictures < 3 cm separated by 10 cm of normal bowel, previous resection → stricturoplasty for both 442; two short strictures confined to the terminal ileum → keyed resection (ileocaecal resection) 436 ×2; three strictures found at laparotomy, the proximal one obstructing → keyed "multiple stricture removal" (treat all of them — usually by stricturoplasty to save bowel). 434
  • Crohn's distal small-bowel resection — incomplete recall keyed cholecystectomy (see the explanation). 438
Notes

Resection vs Stricturoplasty

ApproachDescriptionNotes
ResectionRemoves the diseased bowel segmentIn the index operation, generally preferred — histopathology helps confirm the diagnosis of Crohn's
StricturoplastyWidens a Crohn's stricture without removing bowelBowel-preserving; useful with repeated/multiple strictures and concern for short bowel syndrome. Avoid if malignancy is suspected.
Emergency Surgery
In emergency Crohn's surgery, a stoma may be required rather than a high-risk primary anastomosis, depending on the clinical situation.
1 Crohn's surgery is palliative, not curative — always be conservative.
2 Treat only the symptomatic segment; preserve secondarily involved organs in fistulas.
3 Resection margins need only ~2 cm of grossly healthy bowel — no oncologic clearance needed.
4 Prefer resection at index surgery (diagnostic value); use stricturoplasty to preserve bowel length in recurrent strictures.
5 Map the entire GI tract before surgery; consider ureteric stents in difficult pelvic disease.

UC

  • A chronic disease that affects the mucosa and submucosa, with sparing of the muscularis of the rectum and colon.
  • Surgery is curative.
Notes

Ulcerative Colitis (UC) Definition / Pathology

Chronic inflammatory disease limited to the colon/rectum, involving mainly mucosa ± submucosa; the muscularis is spared. Despite the name, ulceration is not invariably present — disease may begin as mucosal inflammation, with ulceration developing in more severe disease.
Key Distinction from Crohn's
Surgery is curative for intestinal UC — unlike Crohn's disease, where surgery is palliative/symptom-relieving only.
  • Despite the disease's name, ulceration of the mucosa is not invariably present.
  • Rectum is invariably involved with the inflammatory process.
  • In fact, rectal involvement (proctitis) is the sine qua non of the disease, and the diagnosis should be seriously questioned if the rectal mucosa is not affected.
  • The mucosal inflammation extends in a continuous fashion for a variable distance into the more proximal colon.
  • Diagnostic characteristic of ulcerative colitis is continuous, uninterrupted inflammation of the colonic mucosa beginning in the distal rectum and extending proximally to a variable distance.
    • This is in contrast to Crohn's disease, in which normal segments of colon (skipped areas) may be interspersed between distinct segments of colonic inflammation.
  • The entire colon, including the cecum and appendix, may be involved in ulcerative colitis.
    • In contrast to Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis does not involve the terminal ileum except in cases of backwash ileitis, when the ileal mucosa may appear inflamed in the presence of extensive proximal colonic involvement.
  • Crohn's diagnosed a week ago with an intersphincteric fistula → keyed infliximab. 438
Notes

Distribution — Classic Diagnostic Pattern

The rectum is invariably involved and is the cornerstone of the disease. If the rectum is spared, seriously question the diagnosis.
Inflammation begins in the distal rectum, is continuous and uninterrupted, and extends proximally for a variable distance.
No normal/skip segments within involved colon — unlike Crohn's disease.
Isolated proximal disease (e.g., sigmoid/right colon disease with normal intervening colon) is suspicious for another diagnosis.
Entire colon may be involved → pancolitis.
Backwash Ileitis
Severe inflammation in the right colon can cause the terminal ileum to become inflamed — may occur with extensive disease/pancolitis. A cecal/appendiceal inflammatory patch may occasionally occur despite the otherwise continuous pattern.

Workup is the same as for Crohn's disease (see above).

Notes

Crohn's vs Ulcerative Colitis — At a Glance

FeatureCrohn's DiseaseUlcerative Colitis
Layer involvedTransmuralMucosa ± submucosa
DistributionMouth to anus, skip lesionsColon/rectum, continuous, no skips
RectumOften sparedInvariably involved
FistulasCommonRare
Role of surgeryPalliativeCurative
  • Transmural inflammation, skip lesions, cobblestone appearance → Crohn's disease. 441
  • Crohn's — true statement → keyed "usually has no malignant transformation" (rectum usually spared, perianal disease common, transmural). 427 ×2
  • Recurrent fistula, bloody mucus, tenesmus, unhealthy rectum → keyed Crohn's or UC (both accepted). 429 ×4

Work up

  • As in Crohn’s
  • Crohn's with 8–12 diarrhoea episodes a day and flattened T waves → hypokalaemia. 439 ×3

Indications for surgery

  • Fulminant colitis with toxic megacolon
  • Massive bleeding,
  • Intractable disease, and
  • Dysplasia or carcinoma.
  • Malnutrition and growth retardation may necessitate resection in pediatric and adolescent patients.
  • Extraintestinal
Notes

Indications for Surgery in UC

Massive bleeding
Medically intractable disease / failed medical treatment
Steroid-dependent disease
Dysplasia or colorectal cancer
Malnutrition / growth retardation
Fulminant colitis unresponsive to intensive therapy
Toxic megacolon

Fulminant colitis:

  • NPO
    • IVF
    • IV Abx
    • Steroid
    • If no improvement or worsening for emergency surgery
  • Toxic megacolon
    • Emergency surgery
Notes

Fulminant Colitis vs Toxic Megacolon

Distinguished primarily by the presence of colonic dilatation.

Fulminant ColitisToxic Megacolon
DilatationAbsent — severe colitis without dilatationPresent — severe colitis with colonic dilatation
Initial treatmentNPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics, IV corticosteroidsSurgical emergency
Threshold for surgerySurgery if no improvement by ~48h, or deterioration at any timeMuch lower threshold — surgical emergency
Danger Point
Perforation markedly increases mortality in toxic megacolon — do not wait if deterioration or perforation occurs.
Notes

Extraintestinal Manifestations After Colectomy

High-Yield / Frequently Tested
Most UC-related extraintestinal manifestations improve once the diseased colon is removed — except:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)
Ankylosing spondylitis
If already established during medical treatment, these may persist as separate disease entities despite curative intestinal surgery.
  • Mild Crohn's colitis in a young man → primary management medical (immunomodulators). 438
Most extraintestinal manifestations improve after colectomy — except primary sclerosing cholangitis and ankylosing spondylitis.

Surgical treatment

  • Elective:
    • Total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch anal anastomosis (IPAA)
    • Total proctocolectomy with end ileostomy
  • Emergency:
    • Total colectomy with end ileostomy
    • No dissection of the rectum
  • Distension, vomiting, anal abscess, terminal ileal oedema on CT → keyed IV steroids (active Crohn's flare). 439
  • UC 10 years with HGD in a polyp → total proctocolectomy with ileoanal J-pouch 438 ×8; long-standing UC with sigmoid cancer → proctocolectomy. 441
  • Bloody diarrhoea, fever, tachycardia, diffuse tenderness with guarding, WBC 19 → total colectomy and end ileostomy. 435 ×4
  • UC on infliximab/azathioprine with peritonitis and free air → total colectomy and ileostomy. 429
Notes

Surgery

Emergency Surgery — Golden Rule
Do not remove or manipulate the rectum during the acute emergency operation — no one touches the rectum in an emergency. Typical operation: subtotal colectomy + end ileostomy, leaving the rectal stump for later definitive surgery.
Emergency UC surgery: total (subtotal) colectomy with end ileostomy — no dissection of the rectum ("no one touches the rectum in an emergency").
  • Severe UC flare needing transfusion, not improving after 72 h of medical treatment → subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy. 441
Notes

Elective Definitive Surgery — Main Options

OptionDescription
Total proctocolectomy + permanent end ileostomyRemoves colon, rectum, and anus; permanent stoma
Restorative proctocolectomy + IPAAIleal pouch-anal anastomosis; preserves continence via pouch
Notes

Choosing Permanent Ileostomy vs IPAA

Permanent ileostomy preferred when:
Low rectal cancer makes pouch reconstruction unsuitable
Poor anal continence / sphincter function
Patient cannot tolerate the relatively frequent bowel movements expected after a pouch
Important associated disease makes pouch surgery undesirable (e.g., significant arthritis)
Rare Alternative — Colectomy with Ileorectal Anastomosis
May occasionally be considered when rectal inflammation is minimal and rectal structure/function is suitable. Not standard — the retained rectum remains at risk for persistent/recurrent disease and malignancy.
1 UC is mucosal, continuous, and always involves the rectum — rectal sparing should make you question the diagnosis.
2 Surgery is curative in UC vs palliative in Crohn's — the single biggest distinguishing concept.
3 Toxic megacolon = colitis + dilatation → surgical emergency with a much lower threshold than fulminant colitis.
4 Never touch the rectum in emergency UC surgery — subtotal colectomy + end ileostomy, rectal stump left in place.
5 PSC and ankylosing spondylitis do NOT reliably resolve after colectomy — classic exam trap.

Crohn's Disease (CD)
1. General Overview
  • Definition: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting any part of the GI tract, most commonly the terminal ileum.
  • Epidemiology:
  • Highest incidence in North America & Europe.
  • Peak onset: 15-25 years.
  • Genetic risk: 6-10x higher in first-degree relatives.
  • Pathogenesis:
  • Immune-mediated destruction of intestinal tissue.
  • Genetic predisposition (CARD15/NOD2 gene mutation).
  • Environmental triggers (e.g., smoking worsens CD).
2. Pathology
  • Chronic transmural inflammation (full-thickness involvement).
  • Hallmark features:
  • Non-caseating granulomas (seen in ~50% of cases).
  • Skip lesions (discontinuous inflammation).
  • Cobblestone appearance (due to mucosal ulceration & edema).
  • Aphthous ulcers (early lesions).
  • Complications:
  • Strictures (fibrosis causing bowel obstruction).
  • Fistulas (abnormal connections between bowel & other organs).
  • Abscesses (infected pockets of pus).
  • Perianal disease (fistulas, fissures, skin tags).
3. Clinical Presentation
Symptoms
  • Abdominal pain (90%) - crampy, postprandial (common in obstruction).
  • Diarrhea (with or without blood).
  • Weight loss (due to malabsorption/food avoidance).
  • Fever, malaise.
  • Extraintestinal Manifestations:
  • Joints: Arthritis.
  • Skin: Erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum.
  • Eyes: Uveitis.
  • Hepatobiliary: Primary sclerosing cholangitis.
  • Kidneys: Nephrolithiasis.
4. Patterns of Disease

1. Inflammatory (mucosal ulceration, bowel thickening).

2. Stricturing (fibrotic narrowing → obstruction).

3. Perforating/Fistulizing (fistulas, abscesses, perforation).

5. Diagnosis
Lab Tests
  • Non-specific markers:
  • ↑ CRP & ESR (inflammation).
  • Anemia (iron/B12 deficiency).
  • Hypoalbuminemia (malnutrition).
  • ↑ Fecal calprotectin (intestinal inflammation).
Imaging

1. CT Enterography (CTE) (Gold standard for small bowel involvement).

2. MRI Enterography (MRE) (Preferred in young patients to avoid radiation).

3. Small Bowel Follow-Through (Skip lesions, strictures).

4. Endoscopy (Confirmatory):

  • Colonoscopy + Ileoscopy → Aphthous ulcers, cobblestoning, strictures.
  • Capsule Endoscopy (for small bowel lesions).
6. Differential Diagnosis
  • Ulcerative Colitis (UC) (continuous inflammation, limited to colon).
  • Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) (no structural changes).
  • Intestinal Tuberculosis (mimics CD, PPD test helps differentiate).
  • NSAID Enteropathy (intestinal ulcers from NSAIDs).
7. Treatment
Mild-Moderate CD
  • Aminosalicylates (5-ASA):
  • e.g., Mesalamine (Pentasa, Asacol) - mild colonic disease.
  • Limited role in small bowel CD.
  • Corticosteroids (Short-term for flares):
  • Prednisone (40-60 mg/day), Budesonide (9 mg/day).
  • Taper to prevent side effects (diabetes, osteoporosis).
  • Antibiotics (for perianal CD/fistulas):
  • Metronidazole, Ciprofloxacin.
Moderate-Severe CD
  • Immunomodulators:
  • Azathioprine (2-2.5 mg/kg/day), 6-MP (1-1.5 mg/kg/day) (Steroid- sparing agents).
  • Methotrexate (15-25 mg weekly) (for refractory CD).
  • Biologics (TNF-α Inhibitors):
  • Infliximab (Remicade): IV at 0, 2, 6 weeks, then every 8 weeks.
  • Adalimumab (Humira): SQ every 2 weeks.
  • Certolizumab, Vedolizumab (alternative options).
Severe/Refractory Disease
  • Combination Therapy (Biologic + Immunomodulator).
  • Surgical Interventions (if complications arise):
  • Strictureplasty (for strictures).
  • Segmental Resection (for localized disease).
  • Fistula/Aabscess Drainage.
  • Colectomy (in severe, refractory disease).
8. Prognosis
  • Chronic, relapsing course.
  • Lifelong disease, but symptoms can be controlled.
  • Surgery required in 70% of cases, but recurrence is common.
Surgical Treatment of Crohn’s Disease (CD)
1. General Principles
  • Surgery is not curative but aims to provide long-term symptom relief.
  • Goals:
  • Avoid excessive bowel resection (prevent short bowel syndrome).
  • Treat complications (strictures, fistulas, perforation).
  • Preserve bowel function.
  • Preoperative Considerations:
  • Assess nutritional status (malnutrition increases complications).
  • Optimize control of infections, inflammation, and fistulas.
  • Stop smoking (reduces recurrence risk).
  • Immunosuppressive therapy does not need to be discontinued before surgery.
2. Indications for Surgery
1. Failure of Medical Therapy
  • Steroid dependence (symptoms return when tapering steroids).
  • Refractory disease (does not respond to biologics, immunomodulators).
2. Intestinal Obstruction
  • Partial obstruction: Postprandial cramps, distension, weight loss.
  • Complete obstruction: Requires urgent surgery if non-responsive to steroids & decompression.
  • Fibrostenotic strictures: Medical therapy does not work → Requires surgery.
3. Fistulas
  • Enterocutaneous, enterovaginal, enterovesical fistulas:
  • Causes malabsorption, infections, and social discomfort.
  • Surgical repair needed if symptomatic or causing complications.
  • Ileosigmoid fistula:
  • If large → Causes chronic diarrhea (due to bypassing small bowel).
  • Surgical resection needed if symptomatic.
  • Ileovesical fistula:
  • Presents with recurrent UTIs, pneumaturia (air in urine).
  • Resection of affected ileum + Bladder repair.
  • Duodenal fistula:
  • Rare but serious.
  • Requires Roux-en-Y duodenojejunostomy.
4. Abscess Formation
  • Small abscesses: Managed with CT-guided percutaneous drainage.
  • Large abscesses: Surgical drainage + bowel resection.
5. Perforation
  • Rare in CD (<1%) because inflammation causes adhesions.
  • Requires emergency surgery → Ileostomy is preferred (primary anastomosis has high failure rate).
6. Severe Hemorrhage
  • Angiography can localize bleeding.
  • Elective resection recommended for recurrent bleeding.
7. Cancer Risk
  • Small bowel adenocarcinoma risk ↑ in long-standing CD.
  • Surgical resection required if malignancy is suspected.
8. Growth Retardation in Children
  • Surgery indicated if growth failure occurs despite aggressive medical therapy.
3. Surgical Options
A. Bowel Resection
  • Segmental resection (only remove severely affected segments).
  • Minimally invasive laparoscopic approach preferred in most cases.
  • Avoid excessive resection to prevent short bowel syndrome.
B. Anastomosis
  • Types:
  • End-to-end (higher risk of recurrence).
  • Side-to-side (preferred, reduces stricturing risk).
  • Stapled vs. Hand-sewn: No significant difference in outcomes.
C. Strictureplasty
  • Preferred for short strictures (<10 cm) to preserve bowel length.
  • Types: 1. Heineke-Mikulicz Strictureplasty (2-5 cm strictures). 2. Finney Strictureplasty (5-15 cm strictures). 3. Michelassi Strictureplasty (longer strictures, side-to-side isoperistaltic).
D. Bypass Procedures (Rarely Used)
  • Only for duodenal disease (e.g., gastrojejunostomy).
4. Postoperative Management & Recurrence
  • High risk of recurrence (50-70% at 20 years).
  • Risk Factors:
  • Smoking (biggest modifiable risk factor).
  • Short time interval between surgeries.
  • Extensive preoperative disease.
  • Prevention of Recurrence:
  • 5-ASA drugs (moderate benefit).
  • 6-MP or Azathioprine (effective in preventing recurrence).
  • Biologics (Infliximab, Adalimumab) → For high-risk patients.
5. Prognosis
  • 60% recurrence within 5 years (most at prior surgical site).
  • 20-45% require repeat surgery within 10 years.
  • Smoking cessation and maintenance therapy improve long-term outcomes.
Small Intestinal Fistulas
1. General Considerations
  • Definition: Abnormal connection between two epithelial-lined structures.
  • Most Common Types:
  • Enterocutaneous fistula (ECF) (most common).
  • Enteroenteric fistula (between two bowel loops).
  • Enterovesical fistula (between intestine & bladder).
  • Enterovaginal fistula (between intestine & vagina).
  • Vascular enteric fistula (between intestine & blood vessels).
  • Causes:
  • Surgical complications (80%) (e.g., anastomotic leak, bowel injury).
  • Spontaneous (due to Crohn’s disease, cancer, infections, trauma, radiation enteritis).
  • Classification by Output:
  • Low-output: < 200 mL/day.
  • Moderate-output: 200–500 mL/day.
  • High-output: > 500 mL/day (higher risk of dehydration & malnutrition).
2. Clinical Presentation
A. Symptoms & Signs
  • Postoperative fistulas:
  • Fever, abdominal pain, distension.
  • Wound infection followed by drainage of enteric contents (7-10 days post-surgery).
  • Spontaneous fistulas (from Crohn’s, cancer, or infection):
  • Develop gradually.
  • Persistent sepsis due to incomplete drainage.
  • Skin excoriation from continuous exposure to digestive enzymes.
  • Weight loss & malnutrition.
B. Laboratory Findings
  • Hypokalemia & Hyponatremia (fluid loss).
  • Metabolic acidosis or alkalosis (depending on fistula location).
  • Leukocytosis & hemoconcentration (due to sepsis & dehydration).
  • Nutritional deficiencies (hypoalbuminemia, vitamin & trace element deficiencies).
C. Imaging Studies
  • Contrast studies (fistulogram, oral contrast, rectal contrast):
  • Maps fistula anatomy.
  • Identifies distal obstruction.
  • CT scan:
  • Detects associated abscesses & fistula tracts.
  • Endoscopy:
  • Assesses for underlying disease (Crohn’s, cancer).
3. Complications
  • Sepsis & Multi-organ Failure (most common cause of death).
  • Fluid & Electrolyte Imbalance.
  • Severe Malnutrition.
  • Skin Breakdown & Wound Infection.
  • Hemorrhage (rare but possible with vascular fistulas).
4. Management Approach

A stepwise approach is critical for successful treatment.

A. Fluid & Electrolyte Resuscitation
  • Correct dehydration & electrolyte imbalances first.
  • Monitor urine output, CVP, and skin turgor.
  • Aggressive IV hydration required in high-output fistulas.
B. Fistula Output Management
  • Protect the surrounding skin:
  • Ostomy appliances, vacuum-assisted wound devices, barrier creams.
  • Enterostomal therapist assistance.
  • Drainage catheter placement (if needed).
C. Infection Control
  • Abscess drainage:
  • CT-guided percutaneous drainage preferred.
  • If peritonitis → urgent laparotomy required.
  • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
  • Sepsis control is the most important factor for survival.
D. Nutritional Support
  • Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN):
  • For high-output & proximal fistulas.
  • Essential for spontaneous closure & pre-surgical preparation.
  • Enteral Nutrition (EN) when possible:
  • Low-output & distal fistulas benefit from enteral feeding.
  • Elemental/polymeric diets via distal feeding tube.
E. Medications
  • H2 blockers / PPIs: Decrease gastric acid & fistula output.
  • Somatostatin analogs (e.g., Octreotide):
  • Reduces fistula output.
  • May promote spontaneous closure.
5. Surgical Management
  • Timing:
  • 30% of fistulas close spontaneously with optimal care.
  • Fistulas failing to close by 6️ weeks → Surgery likely required.
  • Wait at least 3 months before surgery to allow inflammation to subside.
  • Surgical Indications:
  • Persistent high-output fistula (>500 mL/day).
  • Sepsis despite adequate drainage.
  • Bowel obstruction or distal stenosis.
  • Fistula caused by Crohn’s, cancer, radiation.
  • Fistulas <2 cm in length are unlikely to close spontaneously.
  • Surgical Approach:
  • Fistula segment resection.
  • Anastomosis (functional end-to-end preferred).
  • Relieve any associated obstruction.
  • Avoid aggressive adhesiolysis (reduces risk of new fistulas).
  • Diverting stoma may be required in complex cases.
6. Prognosis
  • Survival rate: 80-95% with proper management.
  • Main cause of death: Sepsis & multi-organ failure.
  • Recurrence risk: Higher in Crohn’s disease, irradiated bowel, or malignancy.
